intro: Piccolo, contrabassoon and three trombones join the orchestra for the Fifth’s C-major finale. Beethoven gives them a blazing entrance, then lets the scherzo’s quiet C-minor music return once more before the last charge.

sections.mNote: A rising triad opens the way to G major

cues.title: Three trombones join the orchestra
cues.text: C–E–G: the opening climbs a C-major triad. Three trombones give the chords a new breadth, while piccolo and contrabassoon extend the orchestra at both ends. Beethoven has saved these players for the finale.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 1 No. 5, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 52, finale opening and added parts. Instrumentation discussed at https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tune moves to G
cues.text: G major brings a lighter exchange between strings and winds. Short repeated notes keep the phrases moving; the opening’s great C-major chords have made room for more nimble conversation.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 59–61, G-major second group, repeated-note figures and divided wind/string writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Better noise than six kettledrums
cues.text: In March 1808 Beethoven tells Count Oppersdorff about his three trombones and piccolo. The finale, he promises, “will make more noise than 6 kettledrums and better noise at that”. He knows exactly what those extra players can do.
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Count Franz von Oppersdorff, March 1808; Thayer, Life of Beethoven, vol. 1, p. 433, quoted by Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.

cues.title: The brass entrance comes again
cues.text: The exposition repeats, restoring the opening C-major march and its full brass sound. The music will travel to G major again before Beethoven takes the themes into less settled territory.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 63, first ending and repeat sign returning to the C-major opening on p. 52.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A concert on little rehearsal
cues.text: Reichardt reports that Beethoven met great resistance in staging his benefit on 22 December 1808. Singers and orchestra come from many groups, and the long programme, full of difficulties, cannot be rehearsed in full. Four hours of music are played regardless.
cues.evidence: Johann Friedrich Reichardt, Vertraute Briefe geschrieben auf einer Reise nach Wien (Amsterdam, 1810), vol. 1, letter of Vienna, 25 December 1808, pp. 255–56. Translation ours. https://archive.org/details/10623218bsb

cues.title: The bass slips sideways
cues.text: This time the repeated exposition takes its second ending. The low strings and contrabassoon move down by semitones under held wind chords. Running figures spread through the strings and then the woodwind; the themes begin to travel.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 63–65: second ending, chromatic bass and development figures passed through strings and woodwind.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: In Lobkowitz’s box
cues.text: The composer Johann Friedrich Reichardt watches the première from Prince Lobkowitz’s box. “There we sat, in the most bitter cold, from half past six until half past ten,” he writes, and concludes that one may easily have too much of a good thing.
cues.evidence: Johann Friedrich Reichardt, Vertraute Briefe geschrieben auf einer Reise nach Wien (Amsterdam, 1810), vol. 1, letter of Vienna, 25 December 1808, pp. 254–55: “in der bittersten Kälte von halb 7 bis halb elf”, and that one can easily have too much of the good, and still more of the powerful. Translation ours. https://archive.org/details/10623218bsb

cues.title: The scherzo returns in whispers
cues.text: C minor and the scherzo’s three-beat bars return. Quiet string notes leave gaps for bassoon and clarinet replies; the trombones fall silent. This little recollection casts a shadow across the C-major finale.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 72–75: Tempo I, 3/4 and recalled scherzo, with reduced strings and wind replies. Eastman confirms the C-minor return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The whole orchestra comes back
cues.text: The quiet bridge grows into a crescendo, and the opening C-major tune returns with piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones. Its later melodies will also settle in C. The orchestra has recovered the finale’s full reach.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 75–76, crescendo and Allegro recapitulation. The second group’s return in C is discussed at https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One of the most important works
cues.text: E. T. A. Hoffmann reviews the Fifth in 1810 for the Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung and calls it “one of the most important works of the time”. He revises the essay in 1813 for his collection Kreisleriana.
cues.evidence: Hoffmann’s review “Beethoven’s Instrumental Music” (1810; revised 1813): Eastman School of Music, https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/; also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven), Reception.

cues.title: An ending with room left
cues.text: The coda gives the familiar figures another long stretch of music. Quiet wind phrases gather players around them, then the pace increases through Sempre più allegro towards Presto. Beethoven still has plenty of C-major chords in reserve.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 86–100, coda, wind exchanges and later tempo markings; Eastman’s formal account identifies the extended two-part coda.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fate by the throat
cues.text: In November 1801 Beethoven writes to his friend Franz Wegeler that he will “seize fate by the throat”: it shall certainly never wholly overcome him. His hearing has already begun to fail.
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Franz Wegeler, 16 November, letter XXXVIII in Beethoven’s Letters, ed. A. C. Kalischer, trans. J. S. Shedlock (London: Dent, 1909), p. 35: “I will seize fate by the throat; it shall certainly never wholly overcome me.” Kalischer prints the date as “November 16 [1801 ?]”; 1801 is the usual dating. https://archive.org/details/beethovensletter01beet

cues.title: C major, again and again
cues.text: The orchestra keeps striking C-major chords, with rests making each new attack count. Beethoven stretches the final cadence far beyond a polite farewell. At last, all the players land on C.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 96–100, repeated C-major cadential gestures and final unison C. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0c/IMSLP52624-PMLP01586-Beethoven_Werke_Breitkopf_Serie_1_No_5_Op_67.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: G major hands back to C
transitions.from: A · C major with three trombones
transitions.how: The exposition closes with G-major chords and a brief rest. The repeat restores the opening C-major triad, C–E–G, above C in the bass. Trombones reinforce the wind and string chords, and the piccolo rises over them. The Allegro pace continues.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 63, first ending and repeat to p. 52.

transitions.title: The second ending lowers the bass
transitions.to: Dev · Running figures pass through the orchestra
transitions.how: The second ending keeps the G-major closing music moving. The bass then slips from G through F♯ to F beneath held wind chords, while the strings carry running figures between parts. The Allegro continues as these figures pass into the woodwind and the harmony moves away from G.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 63–65: second ending, G–F♯–F bass and subsequent woodwind entries.

transitions.title: The scherzo slips back into the room
transitions.from: Dev · Running figures pass through the orchestra
transitions.to: B · The quiet scherzo comes back
transitions.how: The full orchestra sustains G, the dominant of C, before Tempo I changes the metre to 3/4. C-minor scherzo music returns in pianissimo strings. The bass leaves spaces between its short notes, and bassoon and clarinet answer above. Piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones fall silent.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 72–75: held G before Tempo I, 3/4, reduced scoring and recalled scherzo.

transitions.title: The quiet bridge fills with players
transitions.from: B · The quiet scherzo comes back
transitions.to: A′ · C major blazes out again
transitions.how: The quiet wind phrases and repeated viola chords gather into a crescendo. Strings return to the bow; timpani join the approach. Allegro and common time restore the opening C-major tune over C in the bass, with piccolo, contrabassoon and all three trombones back in the orchestra.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 75–76: crescendo, arco, timpani entry and C-major Allegro.

transitions.title: The closing music keeps moving
transitions.from: A′ · C major blazes out again
transitions.to: Coda · The long road to Presto
transitions.how: The C-major closing music continues into running string figures and forceful wind chords. Cello and double bass carry the figures down into the bottom of the orchestra. The Allegro still holds; later, quiet bassoon and horn phrases begin another build towards the coda’s faster ending.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 86–90, opening stretch of the coda, running strings and subsequent quiet bassoon and horn entries.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, IV, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5
source.locator: Printed pp. 52–100, finale; the recalled scherzo occupies pp. 72–75.

timeline.note: Piccolo, contrabassoon and three trombones join the C-major opening.
Strings and woodwind exchange the lighter phrases of the G-major second group.
Full wind and brass chords reinforce the strings at the exposition’s close.
The repeat brings back the C-major march with its three trombones.
The second group’s wind and string exchanges return in G major.
The closing chords return; the second ending sends the bass down by semitones.
Running figures pass through the strings and into the woodwind.
Wind and brass chords gather above the moving strings.
Pianissimo string notes begin the scherzo recollection; the trombones are silent.
Oboe, clarinet and horn phrases sound above the strings. Flutes, bassoons and timpani join the approach to C major.
The full orchestra restores the C-major opening, with piccolo above and contrabassoon below.
The second group’s lighter wind and string phrases return in C major.
Full orchestral chords alternate with quiet wind replies as the coda gathers speed.
The whole orchestra repeats the closing C-major chords and lands on a final C.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
